slices.label: Black Southerners
slices.source: 1960 and 1970 censuses interpolated to November 1968; Black adults in the eleven former Confederate states; the Voting Rights Act of 1965 suspended literacy tests and sent federal examiners, and registration rose from under half to roughly three in five Black adults. The shortfall against white turnout is counted as exclusion.

runs.summary: Rerun with nothing changed, 1968 comes out as it did: Nixon wins, 301–191–46. The closest state was Missouri, which went to Nixon by 1.1 points. Every one of my 100 reruns reproduces it exactly.
howIGotThis: The numbers: the 1960 and 1970 census counts interpolated to 1968 and certified returns; every draw reproduces 1968 exactly before the change.
How sure: I reran it 100 times with different population and parameter draws.

everyone.summary: 48.1 million more adults vote. Arkansas, Georgia, Louisiana, South Carolina flip, but Nixon still wins, 293–227–18. The closest call is Missouri, which holds for Nixon by 0.5 points. Humphrey wins in 0 of 100 draws.
assumptions: Every adult votes. Non-citizens choose like naturalized citizens of their state and sex; Black Southerners like Black voters outside the South; everyone else as their group did in 1968.
howIGotThis: What changed: Every adult can vote, and turns out.
New voters borrow the behaviour of naturalized citizens of the same state and sex; Black voters outside the South.
The numbers: the 1960 and 1970 census counts interpolated to 1968 and certified returns; every draw reproduces 1968 exactly before the change.
How sure: I reran it 100 times with different population and parameter draws.

women.name: Ruth Robinson
women.quote: I've always voted Republican, but this year I'm torn. The rioting worries me, but I don't like how that third-party man talks about colored folks.
women.controlQuote: I've always voted Republican, but this year I'm torn. The rioting worries me, but I don't like how that third-party man talks about colored folks.

men.name: Ernest Reed
men.quote: I'm voting for the man in office. He's done right by working people and he'll end this war the sensible way, not with more blood.
men.controlQuote: I'm voting for the man in office. He's done right by working people and he'll end this war the sensible way, not with more blood.

south-white.name: Anna Reed
south-white.quote: These federal people coming down here telling us how to run things—it's gone too far. We need somebody who'll restore order and let us handle our own affairs.

questions: Election Day is Tuesday. Can this person vote, how likely are they to vote, and if they vote, for whom?
A neighbour asks what this person will do on Tuesday, 5 November. Will they cast a ballot for president, and for which candidate?
Think about Tuesday's presidential election from where this person stands. How likely are they to vote, and which candidate would get their vote?
